articles.title: Peru's updated trade deal with China is now in force, but it does not deliver broad new tariff cuts - Latin Times
articles.summary: Peru's updated trade deal with China is now in force, but it does not deliver broad new tariff cuts  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Peru's Optimization Protocol for its Free Trade Agreement with China entered into force on November 1, 2026, reshaping a 16-year-old pact across digital commerce, customs procedures, agricultural access, supply chains, and investment rules. The revamped deal governs a bilateral corridor that generated $32.6 billion in Peruvian exports to China in 2025 — a 30.1% increase over 2024 and approximately 140% above what the corridor moved in 2019.
The timing is not accidental. The update arrives as new U.S. tariff pressures weigh on certain Peruvian export flows, pushing Lima toward a structural deepening of its most critical trade partnership — one that now accounts for 35% of Peru's total commercial exchange, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism.
The 12-Chapter Upgrade, Broken Down
Five chapters in the protocol cover entirely new ground that the 2010 agreement never touched: standards and compliance assessment, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environmental trade commitments. The seven revised chapters address rules of origin, customs procedures, sanitary and phytosanitary standards, intellectual property, services, temporary business entry, and investment.
Among the most commercially consequential changes are the updated rules of origin, which determine whether a product qualifies as Peruvian or Chinese for preferential tariff access — a technical but downstream-decisive update. The new supply chain chapter creates a cooperation and data-sharing framework around transport documentation and logistics performance metrics, according to the full protocol text published by Mincetur.
The $32.6 Billion Relationship — and Who Dominates It
Mining accounts for more than 90% of what Peru sends to China, with copper concentrates leading the mix — followed by gold, silver, and lead. Through the first eight months of 2026, Peru dispatched $28.3 billion in goods to China, a 39% year-on-year increase, as the bilateral corridor extended its record-setting streak.
In the first quarter of 2026 alone, Peruvian exports to China reached $10.748 billion, growing 42.6% against the same period in 2025, while Chinese imports into Peru climbed to $5.003 billion, up 19.4%, driven by automotive and heavy industry goods.
Which Sectors Stand to Gain
While mining will continue to dominate the relationship, the optimization was specifically engineered to open pathways for sectors left largely on the sidelines by the original deal. Trade Minister Rogers Valencia pointed to agriculture and fishing as clear beneficiaries, given Peru's climatic versatility and China's growing appetite for imported produce. The copper manufacturing segment — including processed wire and tubing products with higher added value — was also flagged as having significant untapped potential in the Chinese market, alongside information technology, wood, and paper products, according to Gestión's reporting on Valencia's remarks.
Former Trade Minister Mercedes Araoz, who led the original FTA negotiations as commerce minister from 2006 to 2009, welcomed the upgrade as overdue, citing what she called low utilization of the trade framework during its first decade. Her comments reflected a view widely shared among Peruvian trade economists that the 2010 agreement delivered far less than its agricultural and value-added export potential warranted.
The SME Angle: Smaller Companies, Lower Friction
The new customs cooperation provisions were drafted with micro, small, and medium enterprises specifically in mind. The framework enables direct recognition of certificates of origin between the two countries' customs authorities, cutting compliance costs and accelerating clearance times for exporters who historically bore the heaviest administrative burden when invoking FTA preferences. Mincetur confirmed that the modernization was designed to serve companies now operating in a global trade environment fundamentally different from the one that existed when the FTA first came into force.
The Critical Caveat: No Tariff Windfall
The optimization protocol does not unlock across-the-board preferential tariff cuts. Exporters who anticipated broad duty reductions as of November 1 will need to recalibrate: what the deal actually delivers is better-defined rules, cleaner procedures, and a new legal architecture for digital transactions and environmental commitments — not cheaper border access in blanket terms. Real economic impact will depend heavily on implementation quality and corporate uptake on both sides of the Pacific, the Peruvian-Chinese Chamber of Commerce noted in announcing the deal's entry into force.
Strategic Context: APEC Shenzhen and the U.S. Factor
Peru's trade ministry has framed the protocol's November 1 activation as strategically timed ahead of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, scheduled for November 18–19, 2026, where Lima intends to present itself as a logistics and services hub for the broader Latin American market.
The original Peru-China FTA was signed in Beijing on April 28, 2009, and entered into force on March 1, 2010. The optimization protocol was signed on November 14, 2024, during Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Lima for the APEC summit, formally ratified on July 25, 2026, and now goes live with all required diplomatic notifications confirmed as complete.

articles.title: "Annual Cap of 350,000 Vehicles": China Concedes on Hybrid Exports Under EU Trade Pressure, Faces Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets and Expanding Local Production - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Annual Cap of 350,000 Vehicles": China Concedes on Hybrid Exports Under EU Trade Pressure, Faces Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets and Expanding Local Production  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
EU summit expected to discuss trade imbalance with China and responses to damage to European industry
China remains optimistic despite hybrid export restrictions, but market doubts persist
Chinese automakers expand European production, facing burdens from production costs and local sourcing rules
Trade relations with China are expected to emerge as a central agenda item at the European Union (EU) summit. As a widening trade imbalance deepens tensions between the two sides, international attention is turning to the EU's next steps. China has recently made some concessions amid the heightened trade tensions, including agreeing to limit hybrid vehicle exports. However, weak domestic demand and high barriers to alternative export markets suggest that reducing its dependence on Europe in the short term will be difficult.
EU Grapples With Trade Deficit With China
According to Reuters on the 14th (all dates hereafter are local time), leaders of the EU's 27 member states will meet in Brussels, Belgium, on the 15th–16th to discuss damage to European industries from a surge in imports of Chinese vehicles and manufactured goods, as well as potential trade responses. The EU's goods trade deficit with China reached EUR 360 billion (about USD 419 billion) last year and EUR 200 billion (about USD 233 billion) in the first half of this year. These deficits extend beyond automobiles, previously the main source of friction between the two sides, to manufacturing sectors including machinery, textiles, basic metals and chemicals. Concerns are consequently growing over weakening competitiveness among European companies and declining employment.
Against this backdrop, the European Commission's policy direction is shifting toward curbing the influx of Chinese products into the bloc. A prominent example is the imposition of high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The Commission conducted an anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese EVs for about a year beginning in 2023. In July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties after determining that Chinese government subsidies had distorted competition in the European market. This marked the first large-scale trade sanctions against Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, following approval from member states, the EU finalized additional tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs, with rates varying by manufacturer. These duties are imposed on top of the existing 10% vehicle import tariff and are set to apply for five years from October 30, 2024.
Limits on Imports of Chinese Hybrids
Under this trade pressure, China has recently sought to ease tensions by offering some concessions in negotiations with the EU. On the 12th, the Financial Times (FT) reported that the Commission was pursuing a plan to cap annual imports of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles at 350,000. This follows an agreement reached during trade talks held in Beijing, China, on the 8th–9th involving EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, among others. The import restrictions are scheduled to take effect in December this year, setting an annual import ceiling of 350,000 vehicles in 2027 and increasing it by 6% each year from 2028 through 2030.
The restrictions cover hybrids manufactured in China and exported to the EU, including vehicles made by European automakers at their Chinese factories. However, Chinese-brand vehicles produced within the EU will not be subject to the import cap. The EU estimates that China's hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc will reach about 800,000 this year. It calculates that the agreement could reduce imports of Chinese hybrids by more than half and lower their share of the European market from about 6% currently to around 3%.
China Confident Agreement Will "Actually Expand Exports"
China, by contrast, argues that the agreement has created opportunities for its companies to expand exports. In an official explanatory statement released on the 12th, China's Ministry of Commerce said, "According to Eurostat, EU imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles totaled 107,000 in 2024 and rose to 302,000 in 2025," adding, "The two sides agreed to expand imports from the 2025 level, ensuring export capacity and stable growth for Chinese companies." While the EU emphasized the reduction in imports relative to this year's projected volume, China highlighted the potential to expand future exports compared with last year's actual imports of 302,000 vehicles.
China's Ministry of Commerce also explained that the hybrid vehicle trade agreement follows three principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. On non-discrimination in particular, it stated, "No measure should target only Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies," and noted that "the import quota allocated to China will be no smaller than the volume allocated to any other country from which the EU imports." Regarding compliance with WTO rules, it said, "China retains all rights within the WTO framework, including initiating dispute settlement proceedings and seeking trade compensation."
Table 1. Plan to Restrict Imports of Chinese Hybrids and the Two Sides' Positions
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| Import Restriction Plan | Set the annual import cap for Chinese hybrids at 350,000 vehicles in 2027, increasing it by 6% annually from 2028 through 2030 | 
| EU Position | A measure to cut imports of Chinese hybrids by more than half compared with this year's projected volume and reduce their market share | 
| China's Position | An agreement favorable to export expansion and stable growth, as the quota exceeds last year's actual import volume | 
Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets
Market doubts about China's optimism nevertheless persist. Observers warn that China is likely to struggle to redirect vehicles previously exported to Europe to other markets. For a start, demand in China's domestic auto market remains sluggish amid weak consumer sentiment and reduced purchase subsidies. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), domestic passenger car sales in September totaled about 1.63 million vehicles, down 28.1% year on year and marking the 12th consecutive monthly decline. Barriers to alternative export markets are also rising. After imposing an additional 100% tariff on Chinese EVs, the United States has tightened regulations on Chinese connected-car software and hardware, effectively blocking market access. Mexico also approved legislation last December imposing tariffs of up to 50% on some 1,400 product categories, including automobiles, imported from countries without free trade agreements (FTAs), such as China. Brazil raised tariffs on imported EVs and hybrids to 35% in July.
Existing major export markets also have limited capacity to absorb more vehicles. According to an automotive market report released in March by global accounting firm PwC, China's exports of passenger cars and light commercial vehicles (LVs) to Russia totaled about 556,000 last year, plunging 46% from a year earlier. This reflected a combination of adverse factors, including increases in Russia's import-related taxes and slowing local vehicle demand. Southeast Asia, which China is targeting as a new export hub, is also a relatively small market. According to PwC, vehicle sales across six major ASEAN countries—Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Singapore—totaled only about 3.5 million last year, while Chinese automakers held a market share of just 11%.
Effectiveness of Local Production Strategy Remains Uncertain
Against this backdrop, Chinese companies are stepping up efforts to establish local production and supply chains in Europe to find a way forward. In an interview with French business broadcaster BFM Business on the 12th, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said the company planned to secure two additional production sites in Europe and was considering France as a leading candidate. BYD has already built its first European vehicle assembly plant in Hungary and plans to begin full-scale operations in the fourth quarter of this year. Meanwhile, XPeng continues contract manufacturing at Magna International's Austrian plant and is examining options to partner with local manufacturers to build new factories or use existing facilities. Changan Automobile has also announced a target of expanding its European production capacity to 180,000 vehicles annually by 2028 and 350,000 by 2030.
The problem is that expanding local production in Europe may not necessarily strengthen Chinese companies' competitiveness. They must shoulder higher labor and energy costs than in China, while establishing new local parts supply chains also entails additional spending. Another uncertainty is that the EU's industrial regulatory direction has yet to be finalized. The Commission is currently pursuing stronger local production and parts sourcing requirements for products such as EVs through the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), while member states and industry debate what should qualify as European-made. Controversy continues over whether vehicles and components produced in non-EU countries such as Türkiye, the United Kingdom and Morocco should be recognized as European-made. Chinese automakers therefore risk having to make further adjustments to their parts sourcing networks and production systems depending on the rules ultimately adopted.

articles.title: Why the Midterm Elections Won’t Bring Back Free Trade - Chicago Council on Global Affairs
articles.summary: Why the Midterm Elections Won’t Bring Back Free Trade  Chicago Council on Global Affairs
articles.full_text:
Moving forward, business leaders around the world will need to overhaul their export and import strategies.
Around the world, businesses, policymakers, and pundits interested in trade issues are eagerly awaiting the results of the US midterm elections. Many hope that the Democrats will gain control of Congress and reassert authority over trade policy, bringing the Trump administration’s continuous weaponization of tariffs to a stop and restoring access to US markets. Council polling suggests a large number of American do as well.
But can a Democratic-controlled Congress bring back the “good old days” of free trade?
Regardless of which party wins the majority, US President Donald Trump is unlikely to abandon tariffs as his preferred trade policy instrument. He has, after all, advocated in favor of tariffs for decades. And since returning to the White House, he has employed every possible legal path to impose tariffs on other countries and gain trade and investment concessions. The use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to enact additional US duties on Canadian goods is just the latest example.
United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer also personally believes in the value of a protectionist agenda to bring back “good” manufacturing jobs to the United States and achieve fairness in international trade. In his view, economic models that support free trade neglect the economic realities of American workers and fail to consider policies adopted by other countries that led to the United States’ trade deficit. Greer argues that “tariffs that directly target the primary sources of the deficit are the simpler, and more flexible, solution.”
For the Trump administration to change course, Congress would have to change or repeal the legal statutes the administration is using to execute its tariff policies and bilateral trade agreements. But given the president’s veto authority and the improbability of a supermajority for the Democrats in both houses after the midterms, the legislative route will be difficult, if not impossible.
The alternative is to turn to the judicial process. But, as we saw when the Supreme Court ruled against Trump’s use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose tariffs, the administration will simply look for other legal avenues. And the game of cat and mouse will continue.
Further, given that the private sector has been the primary challenger of the legality of the Trump administration’s tariff policies, including the IEEPA and Section 338 tariffs, a Democratic-controlled Congress would bring little additional value to the judicial process, other than in providing moral and political support.
Then there is the nonnegligible issue of tariff revenue. This year, tariffs have added $260 billion to the US treasury. Facing a deficit of $2 trillion and increasingly worrying levels of interest rates on government bonds, it is unlikely that Congress will wish to eliminate a source of revenue—let alone replace it with higher income taxes or a federal consumption tax. And, again, the president would likely veto any budget that contains new taxes to cover the loss of tariff revenues as it would undo part, if not all, of his fiscal achievements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
What does this mean for businesses?
Some Canadian firms that export goods to the United States may look to move production to the United States to avoid tariffs and remain competitive, just as Trump and Greer want them to. Others might decide to refocus their operations toward serving the Canadian market, as well as markets in countries and groups with which Canada has functioning free trade agreements, such as the European Union, Japan, Korea, and the United Kingdom. Businesses that depend on imported American goods are also likely to look for alternative suppliers.
US firms that depend on exporting goods internationally are likely to look at moving their export operations to Canada or Mexico—going against Trump and Greer’s plans in this case. Doing so would allow them to benefit from both countries’ free trade agreements with Indo-Pacific, European, and Latin American countries, while avoiding the United States’ unpredictable trade policies.
Still, many businesses around the world—especially in Canada—have waited to see what would happen in the midterm elections, hoping that the results will lead to lower, if not removed, tariffs and more stable trade relations between the United States and its main economic partners. But with presidential vetoes, an “America First” US trade representative, and limited congressional incentive to pursue legal action, such an outcome is unlikely.
Moving forward, business leaders around the world will need to overhaul their export and import strategies. This means finding new suppliers and customers; investing in market development, innovation, and production facilities; and hiring and firing workers as operations are restructured. This is why tariffs are so costly. Not only do they immediately raise prices, but they necessitate spending in other areas as businesses adjust.
Waiting to act, however, could prove even costlier in the long run. Firms that fail to respond to the moment could find their competitiveness inside and outside US markets declining relative to businesses that decided to adapt to the new US trading environment. And even if the next US administration and Congress reverse Trump’s tariffs and other protectionist policies, the firms that have adapted their strategies and operations will be stronger, resilient, and more competitive. Meanwhile, those that continued to wait and see will lag behind—assuming that they are still in business.
The Chicago Council on Global Affairs is an independent, nonpartisan organization and does not take institutional positions. The views and opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.
